FinanceTab.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
FinanceTab.text:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost £10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional £6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's £39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire £39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

Under Labour, homeless figures have continued to rise to record levels and data released earlier this month suggested 177,530 children were homeless in temporary accommodation.

Natasha, who has been living in a hotel in Milton Keynes for the last four months with her son Zayd, is one of those waiting for a permanent home.

The 22-year-old spent the final months of her pregnancy and the first weeks of her son's life living in a hotel.

She told BBC's Your Voice she has no idea how long she will be expected to stay there but was told it would only be temporary.

"I'm just scared when he gets older, when he starts crawling around, I can't even allow him to crawl in such a place like that because it's so dirty," she says.

While pregnant, Natasha says her room became infested with ants, which she repeatedly reported before eventually being moved into another room.

But her problems didn't end there.

While Natasha has her own bathroom, she shares a kitchen with around 60 other residents. She says the hotel is home to a mix of people, not just mothers and babies, and that she does not always feel safe using the shared space with Zayd.

Natasha describes living there as feeling "like a prison". She says visitors are not allowed, meaning friends and family can not come to help her with her five-week-old boy.

She is one of the 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

London will see the largest share of funding, although no figure has been given for how many homes will be built in the capital.

Ministers said Monday's allocation was the first stage of the 10-year programme and more than £16bn remains to be allocated outside London.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested some of the new homes will be built by councils, saying she and the prime minister were "doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Speaking on a visit to a housing development in south-east London, she told the BBC she understood the "frustration of people who are in temporary accommodation at the moment or on one of those waiting lists".

But she insisted that she and the prime minister "are doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Burnham had previously promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period", but the announcement stops short of clarifying how the funding will be split between council homes and those provided by housing associations.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly described the announcement as "sleight of hand", saying: "The small print shows homes won't have to be delivered until 2039."

He said: "Fewer homes will be delivered than previous programmes in this Parliament as social rent is more expensive. Labour have scaled back their affordable housing programme and expect us to thank them for it."

The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election which they estimated would "free up" 228,144 homes for "British families".

On Monday, Reform UK announced similar plans to prioritise British-born workers under 35 when allocating social housing if it were to enter government.

Liberal Democrat housing spokesperson Gideon Amos welcomed parts of the government's plan, but said the plan for more social rent homes "won't cut it" and a programme is needed that "meets the scale of the challenge".

As well as the promise and funding to build more social homes, the Labour government pledged to build 1.5 million homes by 2029.

So far Labour is not on track to meet that target.

BBC Verify has been tracking the target using government statistics on the number of Energy Performance Certificates (EPC) issued by each local authority. Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.

The latest EPC data suggests about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England in the 12 months ending June 2026. To reach the government's target of 1.5 million homes over five years, there would need to be at least 300,000.

FinanceTab.title: US-Canada trade war heats up as Trump threatens to hike auto tariffs
FinanceTab.text:
President Donald Trump has threatened to hike US tariffs on automobiles originating in Canada, as the trade war between the two neighbours continues to heat up.

Trump said on Monday that he will increase tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as auto parts, from 25% to 50% as of 1 January.

It comes after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making unreasonable last-minute demands.

Late on Monday, Canada officials announced a news conference on Tuesday where they would outline how the country would respond to the trade war and work to "protect and support Canadian workers and businesses during these challenging times".

The news conference at 11:00 ET (16:00 BST) will include government leaders in business, finance and economic development.

Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney called Trump's latest levy threat unsurprising and accused the president of wanting to destroy Canada's auto industry. He added that Canada is ready to resume talks only if the US comes with the "right attitude".

The war of words followed several US and Canadian officials saying that talks were suspended with no set date to resume.

Canada walked away from trade negotiations late on Friday night, moments before a US-imposed deadline that would add a 50% levy on nearly $20bn (C$28bn; £14bn) of Canadian imports.

The collapse in talks marked a significant change in tone from earlier in the week, when both sides appeared optimistic that a new US-Canada trade deal could be reached.

Canadian officials have said the US introduced last-minute demands that were "unacceptable", including a clause limiting which countries Canada could sign trade deals with.

US officials, meanwhile, said it was Canada that introduced last-minute changes.

"They wanted more," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview with CNBC on Monday.

The breakdown led to growing tensions as both sides publicly dug in their heels.

On Monday, Trump's tariff threats to Canada's auto industry followed Carney declaring the country would counter his levies with reciprocal tariffs on US goods "dollar for dollar".

Carney said he was focused on supporting Canadian businesses impacted by new 50% US tariffs after the Friday deadline expired, as well as building infrastructure to diversify Canada's trade, which historically has relied heavily on the US.

Carney announced funding of C$11bn ($7.95bn; £5.83bn) to build six icebreakers at a Quebec shipyard for the Canadian Coast Guard that will replace its medium and heavy ageing fleet.

The icebreakers will be used to open winter shipping routes through Canada's northern and Atlantic waters.

Businesses on both sides have warned that they stand to be hurt by the new wave of US tariffs on Canada, as well as the retaliatory tariffs that Canada plans to impose on 8 September.

In Portland, Oregon, Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing say the price of one of their best-selling items - specially designed pillows made in Canada - could shoot up by around 50% to $90. For now, they are holding out on keeping the prices steady, hoping that the "tariff problem" is worked out soon, said Roach.

"It would be one thing if we had three months' notice - that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors," he said. "But when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck."

The rapidly escalating trade war is also raising questions about the other country in North America - Mexico - and the trade pact between the three neighbours known as the USMCA.

Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form. The pact underpins $1.6tn in North American Trade.

Escalating trade tensions mean "the risk of the USMCA unravelling has increased", experts from the Oxford Economics forecasting firm warned on Monday. That, in turn, "would plunge Canada into recession and leave it on a permanently lower growth path".

Additional reporting by Ana Faguy.

FinanceTab.title: 81,000 warning letters sent to crypto holders in HMRC tax crackdown
FinanceTab.text:
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) sent more than 81,000 letters warning cryptocurrency holders they may owe capital gains tax in the past year.

A Freedom of Information (FOI) request seen by the BBC showed the number of letters sent by the tax authority had almost tripled since 2024.

Investors could face fines or prosecution if they fail to declare profits they made from selling, even if they exchange one cryptocurrency for another.

New powers due to be given to HMRC next year will make it easier to target wealthy crypto investors, with one analyst saying investigations will be like "shooting fish in a barrel".

"There is the expectation amongst tax authorities that cryptocurrency investment is rife with tax evasion," says Neela Chauhan, partner at UHY Hacker Young - which carried out the FOI.

"A lot of the traders are young, have had little previous exposure to HMRC and often work under the assumption that HMRC has limited visibility over their activities."

In the 2025-26 financial year, HMRC sent 81,172 warning letters, emails and text messages to crypto investors it suspects may have underpaid tax.

The number in 2023-24 was just 27,714.

An HMRC spokesperson said: "We’re committed to helping people pay the right amount of tax, and the vast majority do.

"We regularly send letters to educate, remind or prompt customers to review their tax affairs, including customers who use crypto assets."

SportsTab.title: LASK v Celtic: Martin O'Neill takes responsibility
SportsTab.text:
In the open air of the Raiffeisen Arena, with bedlam all around, there was nowhere to hide for Celtic or Martin O'Neill.

The Scottish champions had endured one of the darkest nights in their European history.

After going out to Kairat Almaty on penalties last year at this stage of the Champions League play-offs, that is saying something.

Four goals up on aggregate against LASK, O'Neill's Celtic somehow conspired to implode in a second half with little sign of a response on the way to a 5-4 aggregate loss following extra time.

There was no hiding place, and the Celtic manager was frank when put in the spotlight at full-time.

"I'm responsible for this one," he said.

"Without a doubt. Naturally it took me a long time to get over the Uefa Cup final in 2003 but this was majorly disappointing.

"In the context of things, one was a final which it would have been terrific to win, this was a qualifying game which we should have been able to get through.

"We know that we are a million miles from the finished article. That's absolutely true. I think we thought that anyway."

O'Neill was not in charge for that defeat in Kazakhstan a year ago as it triggered the start of the end for Brendan Rodgers' second spell at Celtic Park.

The current Parkhead boss helped steady Celtic's ship last term following Rodgers' exit and again following the Wilfried Nancy saga to guide them to another league title and a Scottish Cup.

This season appeared to get off to a prosperous start until the roof began to cave in over in Austria.

Away from the raw pain of stumbling in such a stark way, the aftermath could be telling for Celtic who now have to not only pick themselves up, but finish off a transfer window without the hefty windfall which would have blown in with the Champions League.

"The qualification for the Champions League is major, it's major in every aspect," said O'Neill.

"Financially, for prestige, but we have to pick ourselves up. That's my responsibility again to do that.

"I think I said last week that if you could qualify for the Champions League there would be players wanting to come on that basis.

"That's not going to be the case but we'll see. Tonight we came up well and truly short, particularly in the second half."

Celtic captain Callum McGregor tells Amazon Prime: "We got what we deserved. We were passive all night. We looked scared to go and win the game.

"I didn't think we were that good in the first leg either. We scored at good times and got away with it.

"We have to suck it up. We apologise to our supporters and the club because there's no way we should lose that game.

"It's as much on the players as everyone else. You can't look for excuses elsewhere.

"You'll now see what people are made of. When you play like that you can't have any excuses whatsoever.

"When you go 1-0 up in the game and it still doesn't settle you, you can't have any excuse and that's on us.

"You fall at a big hurdle and these questions [on whether the squad are ready] are going to be asked. You can't lose by that margin then look for excuses elsewhere.

"This is what it's like to play at Celtic. You have to bounce back, you have to show a reaction and that's what Celtic are all about."

SportsTab.title: US Open 2026: Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz return in mixed doubles
SportsTab.text:
Enjoy it - and do what Serena Williams tells you to.

That was how Carlos Alcaraz settled back into competitive action at the US Open, partnering the American great as she returned to her home slam after a four-year absence.

The tournament's revamped mixed doubles format has attracted criticism for favouring the allure of the sport's top singles stars at the expense of established doubles players.

But the crowds turned out and produced a terrific atmosphere for the tournament's headline act, with about 15,000 people packed inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

All four doubles specialist pairings lost to a team of singles players on Tuesday, while Alcaraz and Williams fell in the quarter-finals.

Seven-time major winner Alcaraz was playing his first competitive match since April after injuring his wrist, while 23-time Grand Slam champion Williams was competing in New York for the first time since she "evolved away" from tennis in 2022.

The pair were greeted by huge cheers and were roared on throughout their opening 5-3 4-1 win against Great Britain's Lloyd Glasspool and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe.

The 44-year-old Williams won the US Open mixed doubles title in its original format alongside Max Mirnyi in 1998 - five years before Alcaraz was born.

Almost 30 years later, Williams still had the competitive desire. She and Alcaraz enjoyed the occasion, playing with smiles on their faces and roaring each other on after winning a point.

Interviewed during a change of ends, Alcaraz said: "I'm playing next to the one and only Serena Williams, so what else can I do? Just enjoy and try to do the things she told me to do."

Their partnership improved rapidly in their first match as they won eight of the final nine games to seal victory.

However, they were denied a place in Wednesday's semi-finals by Italy's world number six Flavio Cobolli and Swiss team-mate Belinda Bencic, who won 5-4 (7-4) 4-1.

While Williams will not contest the singles at the US Open - she has not competed in that format since injuring her knee at Wimbledon - Tuesday's matches provided the returning Alcaraz with valuable court time.

The Spaniard admitted he felt nervous before stepping out on the court - in part due to partnering six-time US Open women's singles champion Williams.

"I think everyone could see I was really nervous, I double-faulted on the first point," Alcaraz said after their opening win.

"I was out for almost five months and I almost forgot how it feels stepping out on the court once again.

"It [took] just a couple of games [to settle] and she made it very easy for me to enjoy it and try to go for it."

For Williams, a return to the Arthur Ashe Stadium was something she did not believe would come around again.

"It's always amazing to be here. I never expected to be back on this court," Williams said.

"It was just a really cool moment. I never thought this would happen."

Sabalenka and Djokovic lasted just 49 minutes, but this was otherwise a day where the singles stars edged out the doubles specialists.

With none of the four doubles pairs making it to the last four, the USTA has the sort of semi-final line up it envisaged when deciding to reinvent the mixed doubles 12 months ago.

Sabalenka and Djokovic turned out to be a very brief experiment. The other marquee pairing of Williams and Alcaraz lasted longer, with Williams in particular catching the eye in their first round win.

But with Alcaraz looking increasingly rusty in the quarter-final, Cobolli and Bencic won convincingly.

The Spaniard was wearing a compression sleeve on his right arm, and the skin fade of earlier in the year has been replaced by a mop of black hair.

This was useful court time for him, but did not really tell us anything about his chances of remaining in New York for the singles final in just under three weeks time.

SportsTab.title: Man Utd transfer news: Will Michael Carrick's side buy a left-back before transfer window closes?
SportsTab.text:
The signing of Carlos Baleba completes a £155m summer revamp of Manchester United's midfield.

At the end of last season, midfield was targeted as a priority area as United looked to build on qualification for the Champions League after a two-year absence.

Baleba arrives along with Andrey Santos, a £48m signing from Chelsea, and £35m former Aston Villa man Youri Tielemans.

It means that, along with England's Kobbie Mainoo, United now have a spread of different attributes across their four-man midfield, three of whom are 22 or younger.

But, at Manchester United, one bad result brings intense pressure.

Even Michael Carrick's calm exterior cracked in a post-match exchange with former Middlesbrough and Swindon Town forward Jan Aage Fjortoft, now a TV presenter for Viaplay, following the shock defeat at Hull when the Norwegian suggested there was a lack of passion in United's ranks.

"Come on, that's ridiculous," replied Carrick. "You played football. You understand. That's a ridiculous thing to say."

So, now the midfield is sorted, it is natural for fans to look at the other areas of Carrick's squad that could do with reinforcements; namely left-back.

Signing an additional left-back has looked an obvious thing for Manchester United to do.

Luke Shaw started all 38 Premier League games last season. He started at Hull. Of United's past 44 league games, the 31-year-old England international has failed to start just one, the final game of the 2024-25 campaign, four days after the Europa League final defeat by Tottenham – and he went on the post-season tour of Asia immediately afterwards.

But, before that, Shaw's injury record had not been great.

Between February 2024 and April 2025, he played as many games for England (three) as he did for his club. He missed three months at the start of the 2023-24 campaign.

There were calf and hamstring issues but also a feeling Erik ten Hag rushed him back too quickly.

More than anyone, Shaw benefited from a 40-game season, allowing him to prepare properly, largely for one game a week, sometimes not even that.

That preparation time will not be repeated.

Although there are blank midweeks between Manchester United's first three games, if they get through two EFL Cup rounds, they will not have a full midweek without a game, other than during international breaks, until the one that includes Christmas Day.

It is the combination of Shaw's injury record and the crush of games that has led to the feeling another left-back will arrive.

There is no doubt the club like Newcastle's Lewis Hall. At 21, he is the right age profile and ideally suited to challenging Shaw for his place, with the safety net of there being enough games to keep both men happy.

However, Newcastle don't want to sell. It would take a huge offer to persuade them otherwise and Manchester United's powerbrokers have proved on numerous occasions this summer they will not be held to ransom, or overpay, for players.

In addition, how much money do they have to spend?

In published third-quarter financial accounts to 31 March, United confirmed they owed £405.75m in outstanding transfer fees, £171.14m of which was due after more than one year. The club are still to outline what the additional $125m (£91.64m) they borrowed in a wider refinancing announced in June will be used for.

The assumption is £70m for Baleba, equal the sum United paid for Casemiro in 2022 and a figure only exceeded in their history in terms of midfielders by the club record £89m spent on Paul Pogba, is at the top end of what they wanted to pay.

Plenty of alternative left-backs to Hall have been mentioned.

Racing Santander's 19-year-old Jorge Salinas has a €16m (£13.7m) release clause, but is also coveted by Atletico Madrid.

Barcelona's Alejandro Balde was left out of the 5-0 La Liga victory over Elche by coach Hansi Flick, to allow him to "clear his mind" amid intense transfer speculation, with United among those to be linked with the 22-year-old Spain international. Barcelona are said to value him between €30m (£25.66m) and €40m (£34.22m).

With a week to go before the transfer window closes, the situation is thought to be fluid, but caution in United circles around the expectations of a new left-back being signed is being stressed.

A significant sale could change the dynamic.

However, the idea of Marcus Rashford leaving has virtually been ruled out with confirmation he will wear the coveted number nine shirt this season, while the anticipated exit of Manuel Ugarte had to be scrapped when he was injured at the World Cup.

Of Carrick's senior squad, forward Joshua Zirkzee appears surplus to requirements, yet with fitness doubts over Amad Diallo – the club are choosing to offer no clarification on the extent of his injury amid a report he could be out for up to six weeks – it is uncertain whether interest from Serie A will lead to a sale.

Carrick does have options at left-back without bringing anyone else in. Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have both switched flanks in the past, while Baleba, a left-footed player, has played at full-back for Brighton previously.

In addition, Harry Amass was Shaw's back-up during pre-season and the 19-year-old remains at United. But he was not included in Carrick's squad for the Hull trip and the expectation has been he will leave, either permanently or on loan.

Most still think there will be another left-back in Carrick's squad when the transfer window closes on 1 September – but it is by no means certain.

SportsTab.title: Liam Delap: Nottingham Forest agree £50m deal for Chelsea striker
SportsTab.text:
Nottingham Forest have agreed a club-record fee worth around £50m to sign Chelsea striker Liam Delap.

The 23-year-old is expected to undergo a medical and sign a long-term contract at the City Ground this week.

Delap's move comes a year after he joined Chelsea from Ipswich Town for £30m amid competition from Manchester United and Everton.

However, Chelsea made him available for sale this summer after he scored just one Premier League goal in a previous campaign disrupted by shoulder and hamstring injuries.

Forest have already signed defender Ousmane Diomande from Sporting for £34m, alongside free agents, Austrian midfielder Xaver Schlager and goalkeeper Steve Benda.

They sold England midfielder Elliot Anderson to Manchester City for a club-record £116m and striker Taiwo Awoniyi to Coventry City for £9m.

Delap's arrival would provide competition for strikers Chris Wood and Igor Jesus, who failed to find the target in Forest's 1-0 defeat by Leeds in their home Premier League opener on Saturday.

Chelsea have also signed two strikers this summer in Emmanuel Emegha from Strasbourg and Danny Welbeck from Brighton.

Delap came up through Derby County's youth system before joining Manchester City in 2019.

After helping City win the FA Youth Cup in the 2019-20 campaign, he scored 24 goals in 20 Premier League 2 matches in 2020-21 as they won the title.

In September 2020 the striker scored on his senior City debut in a 2-1 League Cup win against Bournemouth, and three days later made his Premier League debut in a 5-2 defeat by Leicester.

Injuries played a part in limiting further first-team opportunities, and between 2022 and 2024 Delap spent time on loan in the Championship with Stoke, Preston North End and Hull City.

In the summer of 2024 he was sold for £20m by City to Ipswich and scored 12 goals in 37 Premier League games for the newly promoted side.

SportsTab.title: Luke Littler's Players Championships finals dented by Jermaine Wattimena defeat
SportsTab.text:
Luke Littler's hopes of qualifying for the Players Championship finals in November took a hit as he was defeated by Jermaine Wattimena in the quarter-finals of PC27 in Leicester.

Littler, playing in his first Pro Tour event in 2026, was forced into a last-leg decider, and the Dutchman hit a 115 checkout to claim his first victory in six meetings against Littler on the PDC tour.

The 19-year-old was in a positive mood afterwards though, posting "on the move" on Instagram.

Qualification for November's finals is important for Littler as he aims to complete the calendar sweep of ranking events in 2026.

The top 64 players in the Players Championship qualify for Minehead in November and Littler, who skipped the first 26 events on the circuit, sits in 141st place after claiming £4,000 on Tuesday.

There are seven Players Championship events remaining for The Nuke to get in to the top 64 - including one on Wednesday at the same venue.

However, he has previously stated his intention to only feature in the UK events, meaning he would only have three more opportunities to climb up the order of merit.

Littler is currently £22,250 behind 64th-placed Mario Vandenbogaerde. Victory at one of the events earns you £15,000, while runners-up receive £10,000.

SportsTab.title: PGA Tour: Changes to play-off structure for 2028 a 'big swing' says Rory McIlroy
SportsTab.text:
Back-to-back Masters champion Rory McIlroy believes the PGA Tour are giving fans what they want by introducing matchplay to their end-of-season play-offs.

PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp confirmed on Thursday that from 2028 the Tour Championship will be played across two weeks, at two different courses, and adopt a head-to-head format.

World number two McIlroy, who is a three-time winner of the FedEx Cup, feels the return of matchplay to the PGA Tour for the first time since 2023 shows fans have been listened to by the decision-makers.

"I think the PGA Tour and the Future Competition Committee and Brian and everyone involved have really taken on board what the fans have been calling for and have wanted, which is matchplay," said the Northern Irishman, 37.

"Brian took me through the plan last week for the first time. I didn't really know anything about it. It's certainly different.

"Two weeks, two different venues, but it's cool. I think they've taken a big swing, and conceptually, I think I really like it."

The FedEx Cup play-offs have have gone through numerous iterations across their two decades, presently consisting of a three-event strokeplay series which begins with the top 70 players from the season-long points list.

This week's concluding Tour Championship at East Lake in Atlanta will have a $40m (£29.3m) purse, and while the events have undoubtedly been lucrative for players, there have been consistent questions regarding fan engagement.

McIlroy added: "I think they've been great for players. Obviously we play for a ton of money, and it's sort of like the culmination of the entire season.

"The players have been rewarded. I think what the Tour are really trying to do is listen to the fans and what they want, and I think this idea of matchplay over two weeks is something that came mostly from what the people that watch golf wanted, so I think that's a really good thing."

SportsTab.title: Brydon Carse: Joe Root says he is 'hacked off' and 'disappointed' at nightclub incident
SportsTab.text:
England captain Joe Root says he is "hacked off" and "disappointed" at the incident involving fast bowler Brydon Carse at a Derby nightclub.

Carse, 31, was dropped from the squad for the second Test starting against Pakistan this week.

Images that appeared on social media on Sunday showed Carse in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby on Saturday night and he was briefly arrested and subsequently de-arrested.

"If I'm being brutally honest, I'm really hacked off, I'm really disappointed," Root said in the opening to a news conference.

"After last week's performance, we're sat here and we're talking about something that is not related to it at all."

The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has referred the incident to the Cricket Regulator and Carse was replaced in the squad by Sonny Baker, with the Test starting at Lord's on Thursday.

Carse was not on England duty at the time of the incident as he was released to play for Durham, but he is a centrally contracted player.

Root also said he had spoken to his England team-mate about the incident, and expressed his frustration at the "stupid mistakes" that are continually being made.

"I've spoken to Brydon, and when I first found out my main concern was him as a person," Root added.

"I don't think I'm speaking out of turn by saying he's very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I'm sure that when he gets his chance he will say that himself.

"But I don't think it's the isolated incident itself, it's the fact we keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it's detracting from what we're doing on the field."

In October, England white-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington, New Zealand, with team-mates Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue also present.

During the Ashes tour of Australia, opener Ben Duckett was filmed apparently drunk on England's holiday in Noosa.

And in June, former Test captain Ben Stokes and pace bowler Gus Atkinson broke a team curfew and were present when a member of England's security staff was punched by a Saracens rugby player in a London nightclub.

In this latest incident, Carse was with Durham team-mates Stokes and Matthew Potts, all of whom are under England central contracts. In Stokes' case, the England deal remains in place despite his international retirement in June.

It makes a total of eight contracted players who have been involved in or present for late-night incidents in the past year – more than a quarter of the 30 men on England deals.

When he was reappointed as Test captain, Root confirmed he would remove the midnight curfew which was previously in place during Stokes and Brendon McCullum's regime after a string of off-field incidents during the Ashes over the winter.

Root stood by that decision, saying he still did not think it was "the right way to go", but admitted it would take some time for the team to be trusted by the fans again.

"In many ways we're going to have to earn a lot of trust back, and it's something that we're going to have to live and breathe consistently," he said.

"I might only be in this dressing room for a couple more years, but there is a group of players there who might be in there for another 10.

"We've had a very strong discussion about what's expected of everyone when they play for England, what the standards are that we have to uphold, not just on the field but off it.

"I've made it very clear how we want to conduct ourselves, and now we've got to live it and show people what I see day in, day out in the dressing room, which is a group of characters who know what it means to play for England and not having incidents define how we are seen as players. That's going to take some work and time."

Root also confirmed he had spoken to his predecessor Stokes, who was also seen in the social media video, but only to check in on Carse's wellbeing.

He was asked what potential consequences Carse might face but said he would have no involvement as it is in the hands of the regulator, and was keen to reiterate that he was focusing on moving forward and "building something to be proud of".

"I don't think the recent past has been a good look," Root, 35, said.

"It's our responsibility to change that. I see the dressing room every day and how we operate around cricket and it's very impressive.

"But at the same time, I can understand why we are viewed in a certain way and in a certain light at the moment.

"That's what lies ahead of us, to change that. I just think, if we don't put ourselves in certain situations, it's not something we will have to worry about."

If there was any question as to why England turned to Joe Root for a second stint as Test captain, if he is the right man for the job, then this address at Lord's removed all of those doubts.

Root showed himself to be the leader England need in this moment. Clearly ticking over what happened at the weekend, Root was able to strike the balance between letting his feelings be known, showing compassion for Brydon Carse and not pre-judging the investigation that is ongoing.

There have been plenty of these kinds of news conferences over the past year: someone wearing an England badge explaining a misdemeanour, promising to do better. This time, when Root spoke, his words were plausible and believable.

Some wondered why Root was the one left to face the media, rather than members of the management team like director of cricket Rob Key or chief executive Richard Gould.

Maybe it is because no-one else was able to speak with Root's gravitas. No-one in a suit, not Ben Stokes, nor Harry Brook. Perhaps this is the most impressive display of leadership anyone connected with English cricket has shown for some time.

It should leave no one – especially not the England players – in any doubt where their captain stands on this issue. For any athlete to tell the world they are "hacked off" with a team-mate is a stark message.

Root addressed his England team on Tuesday morning. If the captain was able to speak like this in public, one can only wonder about the sternness of the message delivered in private. Carse would not have been there, but plenty of others who have erred in the past year would have been in the room.

There will be no return for the midnight curfew, but Root was also quite clear about players avoiding situations that could lead to trouble. "Stupid mistakes", he called them. He hammered home the point that players will not find trouble if they do not put themselves in the places where trouble could find them.

But Root also regularly mentioned the notion of this team now having an opportunity to build something on and off the field. Put simply, their reputation in the eyes of the public cannot get much lower, so the only direction is improvement.

Amid all the controversy, English cricket is fortunate to have Root. Not only is he a bona fide all-time great, but also a superb example of how all sportspeople should go about their business on and off the field.

Last week, before his first Test back in charge, Root asked his players to be "good role models and good human beings". They should look no further than their captain for inspiration.

SportsTab.title: PFA Awards 2026: Bruno Fernandes and Khadija Shaw win player of the year awards
SportsTab.text:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw have won the Professional Footballers' Associations men's and women's player of the year awards.

Both were previously named the Football Writers' Association men's and women's footballers of the year for the 2025-26 season.

Fernandes, who last season broke the record for the most assists in a single Premier League campaign with 21, is the first United player to win the award since Wayne Rooney in 2010.

It is a second win in three seasons for Shaw, who secured her third consecutive Women's Super League (WSL) golden boot with 21 goals as Man City were crowned champions.

City defender Nico O'Reilly succeeds Morgan Rogers as men's young player of the year, with the versatile 21-year-old cementing his place in the starting XI.

He contributed eight goal involvements (five goals) and nine clean sheets in 34 league outings, scoring twice, and was named player of the match as City beat Arsenal in the League Cup final.

Arsenal's Olivia Smith retained her crown as the women's young player of the year, becoming only the second player after England international Lauren Hemp, to win the award on multiple occasions.

The Canada international, 22, scored 10 goals in all competitions after joining the Gunners for £1m last summer from Liverpool.

Although it was another trophy-less campaign for Man United, Fernandes enjoyed individual success, surpassing Kevin de Bruyne and Thierry Henry's record of 20 assists in a Premier League campaign.

Fernandes set up his side's opener on the final day of the season against Brighton – and scored their third – to finish 2025-26 with nine goals and 21 assists in 35 league outings. Man City's Rayan Cherki was the second-most prolific provider, with 12 assists.

His haul helped United finish third and secure Champions League football.

In total, the 31-year-old scored nine goals and contributed 22 assists in 37 matches in all competitions.

Fernandes, who joined the club from Sporting Lisbon in January 2020, beat Arsenal trio Gabriel Magalhaes, David Raya, and Declan Rice and Man City attackers Cherki and Erling Haaland to the award.

He is only the second Portuguese to be named player of the year, following back-to-back wins for former Man United winger Cristiano Ronaldo in 2007 and 2008.

SportsTab.title: Noah Anyadike: Cardiff defender becomes youngest player in EFL Cup history
SportsTab.text:
Noah Anyadike became the youngest player in EFL Cup history when he started Cardiff City's 2-1 second-round defeat against Norwich City.

The Bluebirds had just completed their second season at the Cardiff City Stadium when the youngster was born - and that is where he made his debut 15 years later.

Without a senior option at centre-back due to an injury crisis, Wales youth international Anyadike was handed his debut at 15 years and 98 days old.

His inclusion from the start saw him break the record previously held by Harvey Elliot, who featured in 2018 for Fulham against Millwall aged 15 years and 174 days.

But in a cruel twist of fate, Anyadike, who also became the youngest player in Cardiff history, hobbled off with a muscle cramp in the second half.

"It was an incredible evening for him and really well deserved. We've been lucky because he's still in school, so he spent so much time with us in the school holidays," said Cardiff boss Brian Barry-Murphy.

"He's making exceptional strides, and he's a very talented player. We were very clear that he was the best option for this game based on how well he's done."

Anyadike is the third player in under 12 months to become Cardiff's youngest player, following Rob Tankiewicz (16 years and 117 days) and Axel Donczew (15 years and 234 days).

But the young defender from Carmarthenshire is not the youngest player in English Football League history.

That honour is still held by Reuben Noble-Lazarus - Barry-Murphy's former Rochdale team-mate - who debuted aged 15 years and 45 days in 2008.

Barry-Murphy, who spent time as Manchester City's youth team boss, understands the role Cardiff have in developing Anyadike as a person and a footballer.

"I think [we] just [have] to expose him to the level of challenge that he's capable of playing and pushing really," he added.

"As you saw, he's very big for his age. He can play at a very high level, so we just have to keep pushing him to make sure that he keeps getting the exposures and the level of challenge he needs.

"And keep educating him on the parts of his game that he needs to improve because he's so young.

SportsTab.title: Sir Billy Boston: 'A world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'
SportsTab.text:
When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.

For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had been recognised in such a manner; one of its heroes had been acknowledged for their contribution to history through the game.

Sir Billy was a fitting recipient of the honour and a world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told.

You can tell the importance of someone by how many statues have been erected in tribute, and Sir Billy Boston wasn't lacking.

His name was chosen as one of just five to grace Wembley's monument to rugby league's Challenge Cup, while years after his departure north, his home city of Cardiff also ensured his legacy remained cast-iron strong as he formed part of a three-man tribute along with Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman.

Unsurprisingly, Boston is also captured in bronze in his adopted home of Wigan; the place where his legend really came to life.

Born and brought up in Cardiff's ethnically-eclectic Tiger Bay district, he learned his rugby skills on the streets and with the talent factory-esque Cardiff International Athletic Club.

Like all Welsh lads he harboured dreams of playing for his local club Cardiff RFC and hopefully the national team.

Like others before and after for a time, Boston found those routes blocked, having to travel to Neath and Pontypridd to trial before his military service took him north.

It was here where the league scouts came calling, and Wigan persuaded Boston to turn professional in 1953, forever ending his union dreams in the time of 'sine die' penalties for liaising with league personnel.

The money was life changing.

£3,000 could easily buy a house at that stage, while it proved money well spent as he took to the new code like a duck to water, scoring with his first touch in a Wigan A team game.

This prime specimen of Welsh breezeblock had everything; he was quick, he could step and as former player and BBC commentator Ray French put it - his fend was like "being hit in the face with shovel".

The sepia footage and slow shutter speeds of the cameras that captured his magic during his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance.

Whether it was bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston was a blur of speed, footwork and power.

Having swiftly progressed to the first team at Central Park, he would go on to score 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, and tales of his feats would be passed down through generations. There are very few down at the Brick Community Stadium these days who don't know of Sir Billy, young or old, his name carried a cache right until his last.

Great Britain gave him the international recognition denied to him by Wales, and he rewarded the selectors by racking up the tries, particularly against the Australians who would bear the brunt of his scoring ability.

He scored 36 tries alone on his maiden Great Britain tour, dazzling both Australia and New Zealand in 1954 under captain and fellow Welshman Dickie Williams.

Boston was a phenomenal rugby league player, but there is also a powerful message in how in post-war Britain a black athlete could become a hugely popular figure by communities adjusting to a new, more diverse world.

Others like Roy Francis beforehand, Johnny Freeman, and Colin Dixon, also became established names, but never quite sprinkled the same stardust as Sir Billy.

It paved the way for players such as Ellery Hanley and Martin Offiah to charm the public with their talents, while modern day talent such as Junior Nsemba and Kai Pearce-Paul continues to stand out in a sport which has broken down barriers for years.

Sir Billy had a unique unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community.

He was revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.

Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his passing, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.

There was a photo of him and his wife Lady Joan, who had died just a few weeks previously, on her seat with flowers at Wigan's game with Wakefield last week. There is a poignancy that Sir Billy departed soon after her.

His seat will always be reserved at Wigan, and he will be dearly missed but certainly not forgotten.

SportsTab.title: US Open 2026 qualifying results: Harriet Dart and Fran Jones win opening matches
SportsTab.text:
Britons Harriet Dart and Fran Jones both made winning starts to their bids to reach the US Open singles main draw.

Dart, who has twice reached the US Open second round, came through 6-0 6-7 (1-7) 6-1 against Jordyn Hazelitt in the first round of qualifying in New York.

She will face another American 16-year-old, Kristina Penickova, next.

Jones, who qualified for the US Open for the first time last year, will face Germany's Mona Barthel after winning 6-3 6-4 against Italy's Nuria Brancaccio.

But Jodie Burrage lost to Spain's Guiomar Maristany 7-6 (7-1) 6-4, while Henry Searle was beaten 6-1 6-2 by American 16-year-old Michael Antonius in the men's event.

Antonius will face former US Open finalist Kei Nishikori in the second qualifying round, after the Japanese 36-year-old battled to a 6-1 2-6 6-2 win over Austrian Sebastian Ofner.

Former US Open semi-finalist Grigor Dimitrov will face Kazakhstan's Timofey Skatov in his second qualifying match after dismissing Italy's Lorenzo Giustino 6-0 6-3.

In the women's draw, 2019 US Open winner Bianca Andreescu progressed with a 6-1 6-2 win against Dutch player Eva Vedder.

Heather Watson resumes her qualifying campaign with a second-round match against Spain's Angela Fita Boluda on Wednesday.

In the men's draw, Britons Jacob Fearnley, Toby Samuel, Billy Harris, Harry Wendelken and Jack Pinnington Jones all return to action seeking to move one win away from the Flushing Meadows main draw.

Players must come through three rounds of qualifying to reach the singles main draw, which gets under way on Sunday.

Elsewhere, Britain's Arthur Fery warmed up for the US Open with a 6-1 7-5 victory over Cruz Hewitt at the Winston-Salem Open.

Fery, playing just his third match since his stunning run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, came back from 4-1 down in the second set to advance.

The fourth seed will play either Czech Tomas Machac or Dutch qualifier Mees Rottgering next.

SportsTab.title: Serena Williams thrills New York crowd on US Open return with Alcaraz
SportsTab.text:
Serena Williams’ US Open return lasted two matches and one afternoon Tuesday as she and Carlos Alcaraz followed a first-round win with a quarter-final defeat by Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli in the headline attraction of the reimagined mixed doubles competition.

Back inside Arthur Ashe Stadium 1,453 days after the defeat by Ajla Tomljanovic that had appeared to end her career, Williams emerged from the tunnel at half past three to the roars of more than 10,000 spectators. As the 44-year-old American and Alcaraz warmed up in matching purple-and-black Nike kits, public-address announcer Andy Taylor rattled off her accolades one by one to a steadily rising wall of applause. Together they carried 30 grand slam singles titles, a record for a mixed-doubles team at a major.

The tournament was still officially in qualifying week, but the crowds had already swelled to main-draw proportions. The scenes along the boardwalk from the Mets-Willets Point subway station to the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center looked like the middle weekend of the tournament. The No 7 train exhaled bursts of fans every few minutes. Vendors rolled enormous coolers through the crowd, selling cold water and canned soda. Jehovah’s Witnesses stood beside literature carts.

Have you heard the good news? The Open was on a week early and Serena was back. Alcaraz, returning from a hiatus of his own due to a wrist injury in the spring, wore a white sleeve and looked rusty from double-faulting on the opening point. The pair dropped three of the first four games, but won eight of the final nine games to beat the British-New Zealand pair of Lloyd Glasspool and Erin Routliffe 5-3, 4-1.

“I never expected to be back on this court,” Williams said after the first match. “I never thought this would happen.”

That momentum did not survive the quick turnaround, with Bencic and Cobolli ending their run 5-4 (4), 4-1. Yet Williams looked anything but a nostalgia act, flying to the net and reading points a stroke ahead. She even served the opening game of the quarter-final ahead of Alcaraz – a rarity in mixed doubles. When it was over after 55 minutes, Williams might have been second-guessing her decision to decline the singles wildcard organizers had kept open for her before giving it to Sofia Kenin.

This was the bargain offered by the revamped mixed doubles championship: unprecedented star wattage, abbreviated matches and abrupt endings. Last year’s overhaul moved mixed doubles to a standalone slot before singles, cut the field to 16 and raised the top prize to $1m, favoring singles stars over the objections of doubles specialists. Early rounds use four-game sets, no-ad scoring and a 10-point decider. Only Wednesday’s final returns to six-game sets.

Williams and Alcaraz were not the only star tandem caught by the format’s trapdoor. Top seeds Novak Djokovic and Aryna Sabalenka lost in the opening match on Ashe to Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten, who then fell to the married couple Elina Svitolina and Gaël Monfils.

Svitolina and Monfils edged them 5-4 (6), 4-5 (3), 10-8, then kissed and embraced. Both have gone on deep singles runs here without winning the title. In Monfils’ final grand slam before retirement, they are two victories from a trophy and a seven-figure windfall when the event concludes on Wednesday night.

“Happy wife, happy life,” Monfils said.

The revamped event promised maximum attention for minimum wear and Williams delivered both. Her stay was fleeting, but long enough to make the US Open feel as though it had truly arrived ahead of schedule.

TechnologyTab.title: Musk's SpaceX to build $100bn launch facility in Louisiana
TechnologyTab.text:
Multi-billionaire Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX has announced that it will build its largest launch site yet in the southern US state of Louisiana.

Construction of the $100bn (£73bn) project - named Starbase, Louisiana - is due to start next year, with the 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site expanding on the company's operations beyond its current Texas headquarters and locations in Florida.

It will be used to "support thousands of Starship flights a year with missions launching to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond," SpaceX said on Tuesday.

In June, SpaceX shares started trading on New York's technology-focused Nasdaq in the world's biggest ever stock market debut.

SpaceX said it aims to launch its first Starship flight from the new Louisiana base in 2029.

The facility will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region, the company said.

The Louisiana Economic Development agency said the average wage of workers at the base - the largest of its kind in the world - would be 192% more than the region's current average salary.

It will also create more than 8,100 new jobs indirectly, the agency estimated.

"The historic project will establish Louisiana as a global hub for next-generation aerospace, with the capacity and infrastructure needed to dramatically increase launch frequency and expand access to space," it added.

Musk has set out ambitious goals for SpaceX, including plans to reach Mars, develop artificial intelligence (AI) models and launch data centres into space.

In August, SpaceX and Tesla - Musk's electric vehicle and robotics firm - announced plans to build a $16.8bn artificial intelligence (AI) chip making complex in Texas called the Terafab.

The facility aims to meet the companies' growing demand for computing power to support its projects including developing AI and robotics technology over the coming years.

The newly-listed SpaceX is under pressure to convince investors that it will be profitable even as it pursues its expansion plans.

Its shares have tumbled by more than 30% from the highs reached shortly after it began trading but are still higher than their $135 offer price.

TechnologyTab.title: Songs created by AI banned from Australia's music charts
TechnologyTab.text:
Songs that are largely or wholly created by AI have been banned from Australia's music charts.

From this week, all releases must be "substantially human made" to be eligible.

The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) said the new code would help "promote the human nature of artistry".

It follows a controversy around a cover of Madonna's Like A Prayer by Australian DJ Josh Fawaz which recently topped the ARIA dance singles chart and peaked at number 2 on the country's overall chart.

The song has become a staple of commercial radio station playlists and been streamed more than 48 million times on Spotify alone.

Fawaz later added generative AI credits to the song after a backlash.

ARIA said that Australian artists were competing for attention "in the most crowded market in history" and that it was "not interested in promoting or celebrating the success of AI-generated music that does not contain human artistry".

Under the new rules, AI assistance can still be used, but humans must have written the song, and have performed the lead vocal and primary instruments.

AI can also still be used for mastering songs and, for example, using drum machines and auto tune.

Earlier this year a song was banned from Sweden's music charts because it was created by AI.

And in July, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) said AI guidelines would be rolled out in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia for use in their official charts.

The updated code, based on the IFPI directive, also excludes music that raises "stream or chart manipulation concerns".

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said: "These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is, to say the least, a rapidly developing space."

"Artists already use AI tools in their work, the charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists' recordings is a different matter."

She added: "A chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent."

Artists will be required to declare AI use when they submit a song for chart consideration.

ARIA said that if it later emerged music was largely AI-generated it could retrospectively adjust chart positions, and if the piece topped the charts, it may request that awards given for reaching Number One were returned.

Artists and their representatives will be able to challenge their exclusion.

Among the artists supporting the move are Australian electronic act Peking Duk.

Last month, they shared an AI-assisted version of their 2014 hit High on Instagram, captioned: "When you re-record your own song with AI so Australian radio will play it."

Band member Adam Hyde told Channel Nine's Today show that AI-generated music was "removing the human experience from life".

In July this year, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese promised "the strongest possible protection" from AI for Australian creatives.

Albanese pledged that writers and musicians would be able to choose if and how their work was used in the training of AI, saying it would be "theft" if creatives lost that control and were not paid for its use.

TechnologyTab.title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
TechnologyTab.text:
The government has urged social media companies to remove posts celebrating dangerous driving, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham branded sharing them "truly reprehensible".

Earlier Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that "social media companies could take the content down easily and adjust their algorithms to stop it being distributed".

Two police officers died when a car going the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Five passengers in the other car were also killed.

A TikTok account believed to belong to one of the five passengers, 18-year-old Makai Saddington, previously shared videos appearing to show dangerous driving, which have since been removed.

But Cleveland Police said "there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok".

Pollard said the government had "already taken steps" to tell social media companies to take down such content.

He added: "They know exactly what content is on their site, they know how their algorithm works.

"They also know that people post content to get views and the more views you get, sometimes you get money for it, so it's a financial incentive to post outrageous content that gets more people watching it."

Speaking to reporters in Kyiv, Burnham said the people who share footage glorifying dangerous driving are "doing something that's truly reprehensible".

A Downing Street spokeswoman said "the glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful".

She added that the culture secretary has been clear that footage should be removed by social media platforms "in line with their legal obligations", and that Ofcom has the government's "full backing to take action" against those that fail in their duties.

Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to decide whether flagged content is illegal and act accordingly.

TikTok said its policies prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving.

It added that it is actively removing videos and accounts that break its rules, including the account believed to belong to Saddington.

The company said between January and March 2026, 99.8% of the content removed for violating those policies it took down proactively.

While TikTok is taking some videos down, it is not necessarily because it has deemed them to be illegal - it may only be because they breach the firm's own terms and conditions.

There are specific exceptions which are set out in the Online Safety Act, but they can be difficult to interpret.

For example, content showing someone being killed is not necessarily illegal unless it is being shared by a terrorist group, and/or accessible to children.

Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it prohibits posts encouraging participation in high-risk challenges, including driving against traffic, and takes down such content once made aware.

It said it also restrict users under 18 from seeing content not suitable to them, such as posts depicting any sort of reckless driving.

The BBC has also contacted X for comment.

On Saturday, PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

All five of the Passat's occupants - Saddington, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

A video posted on the TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.

BBC Verify analysed the 94 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.

Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.

Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.

Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that".

"It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.

Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a head-on collision in County Kildare, Ireland, after driving the wrong way down a motorway.

They hit a car which was believed to be carrying a family heading to the airport for a holiday. As of Friday, three women and a seven-year-old boy were still in hospital where they were being treated for serious injuries.

At the time, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly called it "irresponsible and dangerous driving".

He said: "What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."

Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live, Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies "step up".

He added: "It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves.

"Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads."

The minister said the government will use powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take down any content that remains online.

A spokesperson for regulator Ofcom said under the act platforms "must minimise children's exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges".

They added that in July, it launched an investigation "into TikTok's compliance with its child safety duties, and we've shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

TechnologyTab.title: Twitch and Amazon face lawsuit over use of streamers' content to train AI
TechnologyTab.text:
Amazon is facing a lawsuit, external over its move to train its AI models on videos people broadcast on the popular streaming platform Twitch.

The move faced backlash from users when it was announced in August - with people having the option to opt-out if they do not want their data used this way.

The class action lawsuit has been brought on behalf of millions of streamers who use Twitch, alleging its parent company Amazon used their videos to train AI without their permission or proper compensation.

Twitch and Amazon have not commented on the lawsuit.

Streamers on the platform reportedly produced, external more than 215 million hours of content in the first few months of 2026 alone.

The lawsuit was brought by Connecticut-based streamer Warren Pandiscia.

It claims Twitch breached its contract with users by using that content as AI training data for Amazon's models without obtaining their permission.

It adds streamers should not have their work commercially exploited to develop AI without consent or compensation.

The lawsuit seeks damages for streamers whose content was allegedly used to train AI, as well as an order preventing Amazon from continuing the alleged practice.

It is not clear when Amazon began collecting Twitch users' data to train its AI models.

Twitch's chief product officer Mike Minton previously said he did not know if users' data had been scraped for training before it gave people the opportunity to opt-out.

He said he was unsure what Amazon "has done in terms of model training and what they've used and not used".

In Twitch's own FAQs about AI training, it said a person's audio might be used to "refine models that create speech to text".

It said this would help improve automatic subtitles on Twitch streams as well as Amazon videos.

Those that want to disable the feature would need to navigate to the Settings tab in their Streamer Dashboard, click the Security and Privacy tab, then scroll down to near the bottom of the options and toggle off "training for Generative AI".

However, the opt-out only applies to individual streams, meaning creators' content could still be used for AI training when they appear in a stream where the feature remains enabled.

Amazon, which bought Twitch for nearly $1bn (£740m) in 2014, has made AI a major focus as it competes with Google, Meta and other tech giants.

TechnologyTab.title: TikTok to pay $400m to US in one of largest child privacy settlements
TechnologyTab.text:
TikTok has agreed to pay $400m (£293m) to the US to end a lawsuit alleging its platform violated children‘s privacy, marking one of the largest ever settlements over the issue.

The deal stems from a 2024 suit by the Department of Justice under former President Joe Biden alleging TikTok and its parent company ByteDance collected "vast amounts of data" on millions of users under the age of 13.

Doing so was against the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), a federal law enacted in 2000. It is the same law that dozens of US states are now suing Meta over.

"Children and parents are better protected today than they were when this case began," assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said.

Other companies to have paid penalties to the US government for COPPA violations include Google's YouTube, which in 2019 paid $170m, and Epic Games, which in 2022 paid $275m.

Meta is also now facing penalties that could exceed hundreds of billions of dollars stemming from COPPA violations alleged by attorneys general of 29 US states. A jury trial in the lawsuit started this week, with the Instagram and Facebook owner accused of targeting child users and profiting from them.

While the TikTok lawsuit predates last year's split of TikTok's US business and operations from its original base of China, the settlement only involves TikTok's operations in China.

ByteDance, which is a privately held company, was most recently valued by investors at $550bn, external.

Under the terms of the deal, TikTok and ByteDance will immediately pay the DOJ $300m. It will pay another $100m when the government vacates a 2019 consent decree, external with the Federal Trade Commission.

As part of the agreement, the predecessor to ByteDance, Musical.ly, was required to pay a $5.7m fine for COPPA violations and ensure it sought parental consent for any user aged under 13.

The justice department did not detail on Friday any action against TikTok beyond the fine. But the department noted that since it sued the platform, TikTok has "undergone significant changes," including to its ownership, privacy practices and platform controls for young users.

When the lawsuit was filed, attorneys for the US said there were more than 170 million teenagers using TikTok and that the app was "directed to children." Yet, it did not effectively gauge the age of users or get parental consent for use from those underage.

In 2024, former President Biden pushed for TikTok to be either banned, or have the company divest its US operations. President Donald Trump went on to support divestment of the app, which occurred last year.

Its US operations are now 81% owned by a consortium of investors, while Bytedance maintains a 19% stake.

A representative of TikTok did not respond to the BBC for comment.

TechnologyTab.title: How landscape gardening is being electrified
TechnologyTab.text:
Part of the soundtrack to a day in southern California is the drone of petrol-powered gardening equipment.

Noise is one of the main reasons that cities around the US, external are banning petrol landscaping tools or encouraging electric alternatives.

These alternatives have the additional benefits of reducing carbon emissions, vibrations and the exposure of landscapers to pollution.

In addition they can mean longer working hours, as they can be used at times when residents demand quiet.

Today, I'm taking part in training run by the American Green Zone Alliance (AGZA), an organisation supporting the transition towards electric landscaping equipment.

To my surprise, the electric backpack leaf blower I strap on is not much heavier than my normal rucksack. Using the blower to herd balls around the park feels fairly intuitive, though naturally I'm much clumsier and slower than the pro landscapers.

As for noise, there's still a buzz, but the sound is higher-pitched and not quite so loud as the familiar petrol-powered machines.

The move to electric power is attracting new companies to the market for gardening kit.

US aerospace start-up Whisper Aero is one of those firms. Its main business is electric propulsion systems for aircraft.

But in 2022, after the Covid-19 pandemic made many people more sensitive to noise, and following a couple of years of research and development, the company realised that its aerospace-grade fans would work well in leaf blowers.

"Our technology is cleaner, quieter and more efficient than other air-moving technologies that exist today," according to Andrew Terajewicz, Whisper Aero's director of air management. "And the leaf blower is the perfect mix of this."

The battery on Whisper Aero's blower lasts up to 15 minutes at full power.

The company has had to scale up its manufacturing volume in its expansion to consumer technology.

Online pre-orders of Whisper Aero's handheld leaf blower started this year. It's priced at the high-end of electric leaf blowers, which are often more expensive than traditional petrol versions.

But for that you get a machine which is less likely to disturb the peace.

"It is so ultra quiet yet powerful, that the brain has a hard time understanding what's happening," says Dan Mabe, the former landscaper who founded AGZA.

Whisper Aero aims to further develop its products, including a backpack leaf blower that would be better suited to professional landscapers.

Even with innovation like that, petrol-powered machines are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, particularly for professional landscapers.

For a start, petrol machines are much more powerful, which makes for quicker work, so less time is spent lugging around heavy equipment.

Terajewicz says that heavy-duty petrol backpack blowers can reach a maximum blowing force of about 50 newtons.

The handheld Whisper Aero blower typically runs at about half that, though it can go higher.

Another big issue is runtime. Professional gardeners like to use their blowers at full throttle.

"For us, it's a little bit hard to use electric," explains Carlos Camarena, a supervisor for a California landscaping company.

Camarena's company uses electric tools where they're required to, in cities with ordinances banning petrol tools. But when they have a choice, they stick to petrol.

His company typically uses batteries that last for about 30 minutes. A crew has six batteries charging at any given time; each takes about 45 minutes to reach a full charge.

Then there's the considerable upfront cost of going electric. One landscaper estimates that it would cost his business around $10,000 (£7,540) to transition all their equipment.

The subsidies and rebates offered by some local governments may not be enough to offset the cost of the switch.

The change would be even harder for landscapers who work as sole proprietors, with a single vehicle and limited space for charging and storing equipment.

Added to that is the weight of tools with multiple batteries, and the cost of accessories to hold them all.

TechnologyTab.title: Is Vine back? Short-form video-sharing app Divine opens to public
TechnologyTab.text:
A new app seen as a spiritual successor to short-form video service Vine has been released to the public.

Much like the original, Divine lets users create and share videos which are just six seconds long and repeat on a loop.

The new app also hosts more than two million original Vine videos and - in a bid to further distance itself from other platforms - bans content made by AI.

Divine's founder, former Twitter employee Evan Henshaw-Plath, told the BBC he wanted to create the app because he felt social media needed "a reset".

"I want to see it rival other apps because I think we have gone awry," he said in an interview a few weeks before the public launch.

He said it was important that there was no AI-generated content on Divine, adding he was "sick and tired of seeing videos and not knowing whether it was real".

"I want to be able to have fun and not have to second guess these things," he said.

At its peak, Vine had more than 200 million monthly active users and helped launch the careers of some of the internet's biggest stars.

Jake Paul and Lele Pons are two of those who made their names on the platform before it was shut down by its owner Twitter in 2017.

Divine is backed by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, who had a senior role at the social media platform when it purchased the Vine in 2012.

It is built on a decentralised system called Nostr, meaning it is not controlled by a single company in the same way as platforms such as TikTok or Instagram.

This means users can potentially take their accounts and content with them to other services that use the same system, rather than being locked into one platform.

A similar approach has been used by X rivals Bluesky and Mastodon.

Divine's website FAQs, external outlines several ways for the platform to ensure all videos on the app are human-made, without AI involvement.

For example, users have to record videos live in the app, rather than uploading from elsewhere, and it will use a verification tool called ProofMode - which works like a digital receipt for a piece of media.

When users record something using a device with ProofMode, it can attach information which helps verify elements such as when it was recorded and whether the file has been altered since.

Users will also be able to flag suspected AI content, and automated systems as well as humans will be involved in looking for signs of the tech.

Divine's attempt to do things differently could also be its biggest challenge, according to social media analyst Matt Navarra.

"The mechanisms people dislike about modern social media are often the same that made those platforms extraordinarily good at keeping people there," he said.

"So Divine now has to prove you can remove some of the addiction without removing the magic."
